subject: physics
question_text: Distinguish between tensile stress and compressive stress.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 9 Very Short Answer Question 3 (printed p.98). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The 1 + 1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: both are longitudinal stress with the same formula σ = F/A; tensile stress stretches the body (length increases) and compressive stress squeezes it (length decreases).

insider_note: Examiners check that both directions of change are named — "length increases" and "length decreases" are what separate the two marks, not just the two names.

steps.label: Tensile stress
lines: stretch the body, so the length
steps.margin_note: Name the direction of change, not just the word "tensile" — "length increases" is what earns the mark.
steps.why: Tensile stress is the case most numerical problems use, so name the stretch and the increase in length explicitly.
common_mistakes: Naming tensile stress without saying the length increases.
Confusing tensile stress with shearing stress, where the force acts along the surface instead of along the length.
steps.memory_tip: Tensile stress: pull it, and it gets longer.

lines.text: σ = F/A both ways; direction differs.

steps.margin_note: Say the length decreases — the formula σ = F/A is the same for both, so it does not earn this mark by itself.
steps.why: Compressive stress uses the same formula as tensile stress; only the direction of the deforming force and the resulting change in length differ.
common_mistakes: Writing that compressive stress has a different formula from tensile stress.
Leaving out that the length decreases.
steps.memory_tip: Compressive stress: push it, and it gets shorter.
